stimulus.text: "That whereas your poor and humble petitioner being condemned to die do humbly beg of you to take it into your judicious and pious considerations.... I petition to your honours not for my own life for I know I must die and my appointed time is set but the Lord he knows it is that if it be possible no more innocent blood may be shed." — Mary Easty, petition from Salem jail, September 1692 (abridged; spelling modernized).
stimulus.source_note: Mary Easty, petition to Governor Phipps and the Salem court, September 1692; public domain.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain primary source

books.section: British Empire in America: Growth and Conflict (1650-1750)

stem: Easty's plea that “no more innocent blood be shed” was answered within weeks. What most directly brought the Salem trials to an end?

options.text: That accusations reached prominent families and the governor's own wife, and the governor dissolved the special court.
That Parliament in London had passed a law outlawing witchcraft trials throughout all the American colonies.
options.misconception: Parliament passed no such law in 1692; the trials ended by the governor's action, not by Parliament.

options.text: That every accused person confessed to witchcraft and was then pardoned by Governor Phipps himself at once.
options.misconception: Most of the accused never confessed — Easty herself refused to lie about witchcraft — and no general pardon followed confessions.

options.text: That a new royal governor arrived in Salem and ordered all the remaining accused persons hanged.
options.misconception: No new governor ordered hangings; Governor Phipps stopped the trials, and the remaining accused went free.

rationales.general:
1. Follow the accusations upward. Background: early victims were marginal people; by autumn the accused included ministers and prominent families.
2. Watch the breaking point. Background: when the governor's own wife was named, the hunt touched the men running it.
3. See what the governor did. Background: Phipps dissolved the special court and barred the spectral evidence it had relied on.
4. Name the pattern. A panic that climbs the social ladder eventually threatens its own managers — and stops.
Remember: Salem ended when the accusations reached the top — the governor's household — and the governor shut the court down.
rationales.A: The trials fed on the marginal — servants, outcasts, the poor — but as the accusations climbed, they reached ministers, prominent families, and finally Governor Phipps's own wife. In October 1692 Phipps dissolved the Court of Oyer and Terminer and barred spectral evidence, and the hunt collapsed. Background: nineteen people had been hanged, including Easty on September 22. The trials ended not by law from London or by confessions, but because the panic reached the men who ran it.
rationales.B: Parliament passed no such law in 1692; the trials ended by the governor's action, not by Parliament.
rationales.C: Most of the accused never confessed — Easty herself refused to lie about witchcraft — and no general pardon followed confessions.
rationales.D: No new governor ordered hangings; Governor Phipps stopped the trials, and the remaining accused went free.
